content.thinking:
I need to be careful not to restate the given figures as if I'd computed them myself — the instructions are clear that the impact numbers were already provided, not something I derived. So I should frame the executive summary and root cause qualitatively, referencing that impact was recorded elsewhere rather than presenting the percentages or durations as my own calculation.

I should also flag key assumptions: provider health wasn't independently verified, the issue may have still been ongoing at the last data point (so duration is a lower bound), response time isn't the same as fault duration, and no change events turned up within the lookback windows I checked.

assumptions: The provider's own health was never independently verified - its failure is inferred from the 503 responses recorded in io-shop's logs.

The absence of a cause on our side rests on the change and flag histories queried (24 hours and ~7.4 days before onset) returning no records; a change made outside those windows or not captured by those systems would not have been seen.
Impact is assumed to continue past the last minute of metrics read; the service had not recovered at that point, so duration and impact are lower bounds rather than measurements.
The time Argus held the incident (roughly a minute from alert to escalation) describes the response, not how long the service was broken.
The pre-onset ClientDisconnected errors are treated as ordinary background noise unrelated to this incident.
Affected scope is assumed to be the account page path that calls the card endpoint; no other io-shop functionality was examined.
input.executive_summary: Starting at 09:15 UTC on 24 September 2026, shoppers' account pages stopped loading. The cause was an outside payment company whose service began rejecting our requests for stored card details; our account page could not render without that information, so the failures were passed on to shoppers. Before this, the page was working normally, and nothing had been changed or released on our side. The automated responder picked the incident up a few minutes after it began, reviewed metrics, logs and the change history, and concluded the problem originated with the outside provider. There was no action available to it that would fix a failure in someone else's service; a fallback attempt to undo a configuration change could not run, because there was no earlier configuration to return to, and the incident was handed to humans to pursue with the provider. The page was still failing at the last point measurements were taken, so the outage lasted at least from 09:15 UTC onward and the recorded impact figures are lower bounds, not a final tally. Only the account page area that depends on the card lookup is known to have been affected.
input.root_cause: At 09:15 UTC the third-party payment provider api.io-pay.example began returning HTTP 503 for GET /v1/shoppers/{id}/card, and io-shop's account-page path propagated that failure straight to the client (src/io_shop/payment_provider.py:95), with request latency rising as calls timed out and retried. No deploy, release or config revision was recorded for io-shop in the week before onset and no feature-flag changes were found, so the fault arrived through the dependency rather than from a change on the service; io-shop has no fallback or circuit breaker for an unavailable card lookup.
